bib.title: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents. Xingyao Wang, Boxuan Li, Yufan Song, Frank F. Xu, ... Graham Neubig (24 authors). The PDF claims its venue on every page: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025". Copy is arXiv:2407.16741v3 [cs.SE], 18 Apr 2025. Formerly OpenDevin ("f.k.a. OpenDevin"). So the ledger's peer-reviewed status and name match what the PDF claims; the filename's 2024 is only the arXiv year. I did not check ICLR's site.

COVERAGE: 103,517 of 103,517 chars, 38 of 38 pages, in three contiguous ranges. References read too. Nothing skipped. Appendices I-K are mostly API listings and one prompt.

CLAIMS

Evaluation numbers: success rate %, avg cost in $ (the column does not say per what; footnote 2 implies per instance). All OH = OpenHands. No CIs or repeat runs are reported.

- claim: CodeActAgent scores about the same as specialist open-source agents on SWE-Bench Lite, without leading.
  number: 26.0% best; 22.0 gpt-4o; 7.0 gpt-4o-mini. Baselines: SWE-Agent 18.0, AutoCodeRover 19.0, Aider 26.3; Tab. 3 adds Moatless 26.7, Agentless 27.3
  setup: 300 instances, no hint text, CodeActAgent v1.8. Baselines use different models. The Lite subset was chosen for cost.
  quote: "OH CodeActAgent v1.8 ... claude-3-5-sonnet@20240620 26.0 1 .10"; "achieves a competitive resolve rate of 26% compared to other open-source SWE specialists"
  where: p7-8, Tab. 3-4

- claim: The same agent spans three task categories, which is the paper's central result: generality, not top scores.
  number: none
  setup: authors' reading of Tab. 3 (CodeAct on software, web via delegation, GPQA). The GAIA figure comes from GPTSwarm, not CodeAct.
  quote: "the same CodeAct agent, without any modifications to its system prompt, demonstrates competitive performance across three major task categories"
  where: p7

- claim: Running the full evaluation on every change is too costly.
  number: $6.9k full SWE-Bench (2294 instances, $3 each, an estimate); about $600 for Lite with gpt-4o
  setup: authors' estimates
  quote: "Running the complete set of 2294 instances costs $6.9k, using a conservative estimate of $3 per instance."; "Running a SWE-Bench Lite Jimenez et al. (2024) evaluation withgpt-4o costs around 600 USD."
  where: p7 fn2; p19 fn4

- claim: Agent regressions are caught with end-to-end tests that mock the LLM, matching exact prompts and comparing output to gold files.
  number: none reported (no bug counts or coverage figure)
  setup: run on every PR and on main commits; Linux and Mac; local, SSH and exec sandboxes. Substantial changes regenerate responses with real LLMs.
  quote: "the framework intercepts all LLM calls and supplies predefined responses based on exact prompt matches"
  where: p19, §E

- claim: The architecture is an agent mapping history to an action, a runtime mapping an action to an observation, and an event stream recording both.
  number: 3 components
  setup: design description, no ablation
  quote: "OpenHands consists of 3 main components: 1) Agent abstraction ... 2) Event stream for tracking history of actions and observations; 3) Runtime to execute all actions into observations"
  where: p3, Fig. 2

- claim: Each task session gets its own Docker container with a bash shell, Jupyter IPython server and Playwright Chromium, reached through a REST API inside it. A workspace directory is mounted in.
  number: none
  setup: design description. "Securely isolated" is asserted, never tested.
  quote: "For each task session, OpenHands spins up a securely isolated docker container sandbox, where all the actions from the event stream are executed."
  where: p4, §2.2; p20-22, App. F

- claim: A new tool is added only if the LLM cannot easily write the code itself, or if it calls an external model.
  number: none
  setup: stated policy for AgentSkills (17 functions listed as of v0.6, my count), no evaluation
  quote: "We only add a new skill when: (1) it is not readily achievable for LLM to write code directly ... and/or (2) it involves calling an external model"
  where: p5, §2.3; p23-26, App. I

- claim: Runtime images get a content-hash tag for reproducibility and a generic tag for the latest build.
  number: none
  setup: MD5 of the build folder; reuse order is exact hash, then generic image as base, then from scratch
  quote: "Identical hash tags guarantee that the images were built with exactly the same source code and Dockerfile"
  where: p21

- claim: HumanEvalFix: OH is below SWE-agent, which had a 1-shot demonstration from the test set.
  number: OH 79.3 gpt-4o ($0.14), 20.1 gpt-3.5 ($0.11); SWE-agent 87.7 gpt-4-turbo; prompting 16.6 BLOOMZ, 30.4 OctoCoder, 47.5 DeepSeekCoder, 48.6 StarCoder2
  setup: 164 instances, Python split, pass@k, OH v1.5 0-shot
  quote: "OpenHands CodeActAgent successfully fixes 79.3% of bugs in the Python split"; "SWE-agent, 1-shot (Yang et al., 2024) gpt-4-turbo 87.7"
  where: p7-8

- claim: ML-Bench: OH leads, but only with gpt-4o.
  number: OH 76.5 gpt-4o ($0.25), 58.8 gpt-4-1106 ($1.22), 13.2 gpt-3.5 ($0.12); Aider 64.4; SWE-Agent 42.6; BM25 prompting 11.0/22.1/26.2
  setup: 68 instances ("quarter subset"), v1.5
  quote: "gpt-4o-2024-05-13 76.5 0 .25"
  where: p8

- claim: Other software benchmarks, OH v1.5. BIRD and BioCoder lead their tables; ToolQA leads only with gpt-4o; Gorilla trails the finetuned baseline.
  number: BIRD 47.3 gpt-4o, 42.7 gpt-4-1106 (baselines 18.3, 31.3). BioCoder 27.5 (11.0, 12.7). Gorilla 36.4 gpt-4o, 21.6 gpt-3.5 (Gorilla finetuned llama-7b 75.0; prompting 8.7, 21.2, 29.7). ToolQA 47.2 gpt-4o, 2.3 gpt-3.5 (ReAct 43.1, 36.8; prompting 5.1, 5.6, 10.6)
  setup: BIRD 300 dev samples, multi-turn. BioCoder 157 Python, context removed from prompts. Gorilla 1775. ToolQA 800, easy subset only.
  quote: "OH CodeActAgent v1.5 gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 2.3 0 .03gpt-4o-2024-05-13 47.2 0 .91"; "OH CodeActAgent v1.5 gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 21.6 0 .002gpt-4o-2024-05-13 36.4 0 .04"
  where: p8-9

- claim: Web results are low and trail trained or specialised baselines.
  number: WebArena OH BrowsingAgent 15.5 claude ($0.10), 14.8 gpt-4o ($0.15), 8.5 mini ($0.01); CodeAct via delegation 15.3/14.5/8.3. Baselines Auto Eval & Refine 20.2, AutoWebGLM 18.2, WebArena Agent 14.4 gpt-4-turbo and 6.2 gpt-3.5, Patel 9.4, Lemur 5.3. MiniWoB++ OH 40.8 gpt-4o, 27.2 gpt-3.5, delegation 39.8; CC-NET 91.1; WGE 34.6
  setup: WebArena 812 instances; MiniWoB++ 125 environments, full set, including vision-dependent tasks
  quote: "claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 15.5 0 .10"; "OH BrowsingAgent v1.0 gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 27.2 0 .01gpt-4o-2024-05-13 40.8 0 .05"
  where: p9, Tab. 5

- claim: Delegating browsing from CodeAct costs almost nothing against calling BrowsingAgent directly (at most 1.0 point, my subtraction).
  number: 15.3 vs 15.5; 14.5 vs 14.8; 8.3 vs 8.5; 39.8 vs 40.8
  setup: Tab. 5; v1.8 via BrowsingAgent v1.0. Same sub-agent both ways, so this is not a test of multi-agent benefit.
  quote: "OH CodeActAgent v1.8 via delegation to BrowsingAgent v1.0 gpt-4o-2024-05-13 39.8"
  where: p9

- claim: Misc. assistance is mixed: GPQA, GAIA, AgentBench and MINT math lead; MINT code, ProofWriter and EDA do not.
  number: GPQA diamond 52.0 claude v1.8 ($0.065), against GPT-4 CoT 38.8, expert 81.3, non-expert 21.9. GAIA GPTSwarm 32.1 gpt-4o ($0.050), 30.2 gpt-4-0125 ($0.110), AutoGPT 13.2. AgentBench 57.6 gpt-4o, 11.8 gpt-3.5 (baseline 42.4, 32.6). MINT math 77.3, 33.8 (65.8). MINT code 50.0, 5.2 (59.6). ProofWriter 78.8 (Logic-LM 79.6, CoT 68.1). EDA 38.0, 24.0 (40.0, 27.0)
  setup: GPQA 198. GAIA L1 validation only, 53. AgentBench OS subset 144. MINT math 225, code 136, up to 5 iterations. ProofWriter 600, 5-hop, using Logic-LM's logical forms. EDA 200 (100 Things + 100 Celebrities). v1.5 except GPQA and GPTSwarm.
  quote: "OH CodeActAgent v1.8 claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 52.0 0 .065"; "OH GPTSwarm v1.0 gpt-4-0125-preview 30.2 0 .110gpt-4o-2024-05-13 32.1 0 .050"
  where: p10, Tab. 6

- claim: GPQA across subsets, OH v1.5 with gpt-4o: diamond 53.1, main 49.3, extended 52.8.
  number: $0.054 avg; GPT4-turbo 51.8/47.4/42.4 at $0.501; GPT-3.5 27.9/23.4/26.1 at $0.012; GPT-4 with search 38.8/41.0/39.4
  setup: Tab. 7, GPQA subsets
  quote: "OpenHands + CodeActAgent v1.5 + GPT4o 53.1 49.3 52.8 0.054"
  where: p23

- claim: Model choice moves results more than anything else shown; the same agent spans wide ranges across models.
  number: my reading of 2.3 to 47.2 on ToolQA; 5.2 to 50.0 on MINT code
  setup: Tab. 4 and 6; quotes above. Observation only, the paper does not state this.
  quote: "OH CodeActAgent v1.5 gpt-4o-2024-05-13 50.0 0 .087gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613 5.2 0 .030"
  where: p10

- claim: Project traction at time of writing.
  number: 32K stars, 2.1K contributions, 188 contributors, 15 benchmarks, over 10 agents
  setup: snapshot, self-reported
  quote: "with 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors"
  where: p3

LIMITS
- Conceded: "Current agents still struggle with complex tasks" and "Current agent suffers a lot when editing long files" (p17-18). Workflow "still requires a substantial hand-crafted workload" (p18). Agents "lack the ability to perform complex, long-horizon tasks in the real world reliably" (p18). Multi-modality is limited to predefined skills.
- Does not show (my reading):
  - No ablation, so nothing links the event stream, runtime or AgentSkills to any score.
  - No sandbox evaluation: no escape, prompt-injection or side-effect test, and no isolation comparison. Safety is argued only in the ethics statement.
  - No variance, CIs, significance tests or repeat runs. On a 300-instance set, 26.0 vs 27.3 is about 4 instances (my arithmetic).
  - Most comparisons mix models and possibly setups; the paper does not say baselines were re-run. Same-model comparisons are rare.
  - Mixed agent versions (v1.5 and v1.8).
  - Subsets throughout: SWE Lite, ML-Bench quarter, ToolQA easy, GAIA L1, BIRD 300 sample.
  - No measure of the integration tests' effectiveness, of human-AI collaboration, or of the productivity it mentions.
- "Without any modifications to its system prompt" needs care: App. K adds a concise-answer instruction to the browsing agent for WebArena, and App. H describes a separate CodeActSWEAgent with an in-context demonstration.
- Dated: models (gpt-4o-2024-05-13, claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, gpt-4o-mini), star counts, runtime tag v0.9.3, skills at v0.6, the `agenthub` path, and the line-based `edit_file`.

BUILDS ON: CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024a), action space; SWE-Agent (Yang et al., 2024), Agent-Computer Interface and editing tools; Aider (Gauthier), editing; BrowserGym (ServiceNow; Drouin et al., 2024), browser DSL; integration testing (Leung & White, 1990); GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024); WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023a); pass@k (Chen et al., 2021). Inspired by Devin (Cognition.ai).

CODE
- Abstraction, p3 Fig. 2 (garbled spacing normalised, words unchanged): `Agent : Event History -> Action`; `Runtime : Action -> Observation`
- Agent loop signature, p4 Fig. 3: `def step(self, state: State):` then `for prev_action, obs in state.history:` then `response = self.llm.do_completion(messages)`; returns `AgentFinishAction()`, `CmdRunAction(command=action.command)`, `IPythonRunCellAction(code=action.code)`, `BrowseInteractiveAction(code=action.code)` or `MessageAction(content=action.message)`.
- Edit tool, p24: `def edit_file(start: int, end: int, content: str) -> None:`

FIGURES
- Fig. 2, p3: "OpenHands consists of 3 main components..." Shows a real trajectory beside the agent/event-stream/runtime split. Best candidate; the loop is quicker to see than to read.
- Fig. 3, p4: "Minimal example of implementing an agent in OpenHands." Whole agent in about 25 lines, showing how thin the agent is against the harness.
- Fig. 4, p20: "OpenHands runtime workflow." Backend, REST and container path.
- Fig. 5, p22: "OpenHands Runtime Image Build Workflow." Too detailed unless image caching is being taught.
- Fig. 1, p2: UI screenshot. Low value.

NOTE FIT (asked for; I read lines 1-80 of 02 and 1-60 of 04, and only filenames for the rest)
- 02-harness-anatomy is the right primary. The three-part split and event stream give a concrete instance of its Tools, Environment and State subsystems, and the note's sources are currently mostly blogs.
- 04-execution-boundaries is a secondary fit: per-session container, API inside the sandbox, mounted workspace, arbitrary base images. It offers a design example only, no evidence that isolation holds, so it cannot back a safety claim.
- By filename: 03-tool-design (skill inclusion rule, §2.3), 05-verification-loops (mocked-LLM tests, App. E), 07-orchestration (AgentDelegateAction, thin).

PROBLEMS
- Internal inconsistencies:
  - CodeAct gpt-4o-mini on SWE-Bench Lite is 6.3 in Tab. 3 ("gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 6.3 8.3") but 7.0 in Tab. 4.
  - Expert human GPQA diamond is 81.3 in Tab. 6 but 81.2 in Tab. 7.
  - Tab. 3's 53.1 GPQA is footnoted as v1.5 under a v1.8 heading.
  - BioCoder is cited as Tang 2024b in Tab. 4 and 2024c elsewhere.
  - Fig. 3 says `BrowseInteractiveAction`, the text says `BrowserInteractiveAction`.
- Overstatement: "almost doubling the performance of StarCoder2-15B" (p7), yet 79.3 / 48.6 is about 1.63x. Do not repeat the phrase.
- Tab. 4 omits Moatless and Agentless, the two rows beating OH in Tab. 3, though the prose claim cites Tab. 4.
- Tab. 4's ToolQA baseline "gpt-3 43.1" is printed that way; I could not confirm the label.
- Extraction: tables are flattened, with merged rows and spaced costs ("0 .11"), and I mapped values to rows by order. Check Tab. 4-6 against the page before citing. Fig. 2 text is garbled. Table 1's checkmarks extract as " and % glyphs (OH is the only row with all marks).
- Embedded instructions: none aimed at the reader. App. K contains an example agent prompt ("Do not ask me for confirmation at any point"), which is sample content and was not acted on.
